title: After burning through four weekly Astra limits, I finally brought my childhood MMO to the browser
author: Suspicious-Trouble97
selftext:
17 years ago, when I was 14, I ran a Tales of Pirates private server called One Piece Online.

The community had made the server source available, and that gave me a starting point. The setup I used back then was C++ running on Windows Server 2003. Now I'm coming back to it with a different idea of what I want to build.

I've burned through the equivalent of four weekly Astra usage limits getting here. Luckily, I had access to usage resets, which let me keep going. The result so far is Corals, a playable browser alpha built from that old project.

I replaced the old C++ client with a browser client, rebuilt the database layer around PostgreSQL, and moved the backend to Linux. Getting accounts, character persistence and gameplay working together again has been a big part of the work.

A big part of my workflow was using /goal to give Astra time to dig through the old code and work out how the game's systems fit together. The longest of those runs lasted 36 hours. Before rebuilding a mechanic, I needed to understand what the existing code was actually doing. Those long runs helped me work through that, system by system.

I'm keeping the original assets and core mechanics as a foundation. From there, I want to build my own lore and change the gameplay into something I always felt was missing from the original.

Sailing is a good example. I always found the old navigation mechanics a bit too simple. I found a project called Open Ocean on GitHub and have been using it, with Astra's help, to rework that part of the game. That's the kind of change I want to make throughout Corals: take the starting point I already have and see how much further I can develop it.

The video shows where the alpha is today: previewing classes, visiting the blacksmith, exploring, fighting in the snowy forest and sailing out of the harbor. I cut the waiting around, but kept the gameplay at its original speed. There's still plenty of work to do on the game.

There's something pretty strange about returning to a project from when you were 14 and finally being able to build the ideas you had for it. That's what this project is for me.

Has anyone here used AI to come back to an old game project? How far did you end up taking it from the original?

You can try the current alpha here: [https://antoinecarle.itch.io/corals](https://antoinecarle.itch.io/corals)

If you'd like to see where this goes, you can follow me on [itch.io](http://itch.io) too. I'll be sharing updates there as I keep working on Corals. And if you give it a try, I'd love to hear what you think.

comments.author: AshenThroneDev
comments.body:
Porting an old single-server MMO onto Postgres is a brave one. The thing that bit us running a browser MMO on Postgres (Ashen Throne): once more than one thing can touch the same player row, like a tick loop plus request handlers, every "read, check, then write" has to lock the row inside a transaction, or you get duplicated items that only show up under real load. The old single-threaded server never had to care, so it's worth hunting for that pattern in the ported code early.

Also +1 on letting the model read the old code for hours before touching anything. Our best sessions were the ones where it wrote down the implicit rules first and then built against them.

replies.author: Odd_Campaign_8134
replies.body: Did you end up using SELECT FOR UPDATE on the player rows, or did you go with something heavier like advisory locks? Curious because I'd imagine the tick loop touching every active player in one transaction could get ugly fast if you lock too granularly.

replies.author: AshenThroneDev
replies.body:
Both, for different jobs. Row-level SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a short transaction for anything that reads, checks and then writes a player's stuff, and a single advisory lock only to elect one tick leader, so two server processes can never both run the tick.

And yeah, never one transaction across every active player. Keep tick work in short transactions, and where a step touches many players, give each one its own, so one slow player can't hold everyone else's locks. The other rule that saved us: always lock in the same order (for us the commander row, then troops, then hospital rows, sorted by id). Two code paths locking the same rows in opposite order is where the deadlocks come from.

replies.author: Suspicious-Trouble97
replies.body:
Thanks for sharing this, it's really useful to hear from someone who's dealt with it on another browser MMO.



The original source already handled all gameplay calculations on the server, and I've kept that architecture. Damage, item transactions and other game logic are calculated and validated server-side, with the results sent back to the client and the relevant changes persisted to PostgreSQL.



I've also had agents run a lot of tests specifically trying to break those systems. They uncovered issues that helped me improve the validation and transaction handling. Your point about concurrent writes is a good one though. Keeping the calculations on the server doesn't automatically prevent database race conditions, so I'll take a closer look at the pattern you mentioned.
